classifications.label: Instruments measure fundamentally different physical quantities or regimes
Measurement noise dominates signal; instruments are not yet locked to true time evolution
Systematic calibration drift or environmental gradient not yet captured; baselines are unstable or instrument responses are time-dependent
Laboratory and observational instruments are coupled through a shared noise source (e.g., vibration, electromagnetic pickup, environmental fluctuation) that masks independent physical signals

Instruments measure fundamentally different physical quantities, regimes, or bandwidths; lab and obs streams are orthogonal or decorrelated by design or by environmental coupling to different subsystems

Measurement noise dominates signal; instruments report quasi-random walks (white or pink noise) rather than phase-locked responses to environmental oscillations; true signal is below instrument resolution or settlement is not oscillating at the frequencies these instruments detect

Baseline window (days 1–10) is too short to capture instrument warm-up, stabilization, or environmental transient; true instrument baselines are still evolving, and post-baseline measurements (days 11–20) are contaminated by slow instrument drift or environmental trend not yet visible in variance

Lab instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) are contaminated by building vibration or electromagnetic noise; obs instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) measure environmental response (wind, thermal); both are driven by a common weak external signal, but the lab/obs noise sources decouple them

Residual: instrument calibration constants or gain settings are inconsistent or misaligned between lab and obs versions of the same instrument type; what is labeled 'resonator_lab' and 'resonator_obs' are actually measuring different instrumental parameters (e.g., one measures resonance frequency, the other resonance Q-factor), masquerading as the same measurement
The r=0.516 pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation is a noise-fitting artifact from exhaustive lag search; no true signal coupling exists.

Measurement noise dominates signal across all four streams; instruments report quasi-random walks with no phase-locking to environment; true signal is below resolution or settlement is not oscillating at detected frequencies.

Baseline window (days 1–10) is too short; instruments and environment have intrinsic timescales of 10–20 days; post-baseline measurements are contaminated by slow instrument drift, thermal transient, or environmental cycle not yet resolved.

Lab instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) are contaminated by a shared local noise source (building vibration, AC hum, electromagnetic coupling); obs instruments measure environment (wind, thermal); the anomalous r=0.516 pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation reflects cross-coupling of lab vibration into resonator_obs via a 3-day phase lag (e.g., resonator_obs is resonantly damped).

Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs are actually measuring different instrumental parameters than their nominal 'twin' streams (pendulum_obs, resonator_lab); the anomalous r=0.516 correlation reflects a real but misidentified physical coupling between two non-equivalent instruments.

Pendulum_obs experienced a genuine physical change around day 23: thermal drift, component fatigue, environmental shock, or calibration drift in the sensor itself. Other instruments did not because they have different thermal time constants or mounting locations.

The level shift in pendulum_obs is a measurement artifact: a human error in trial recording, a software glitch in the data acquisition system, or a one-time recalibration of the sensor at day 23 that was not documented. The true physical behavior of the instrument is unchanged.

Pendulum_obs is measuring a different physical quantity than pendulum_lab (e.g., amplitude vs. period, or damped vs. undamped oscillation); the day-23 shift reflects a real change in the environment's effect on that quantity, while pendulum_lab (measuring the other parameter) remains stable. Cross-instrument correlations are weak because they track different measurands.

The settlement or its local environment experienced a discrete environmental shock or change around day 23 (seismic, pressure, thermal) that affected pendulum_obs's measurement directly or its mounting, but not the other instruments because they are differently located, oriented, or damped. The r=0.516 pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs anomaly is unrelated and remains a search artifact.

The r=0.516 pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs anomaly is real (not a search artifact), reflecting a true 3-day phase-lagged coupling, and the day-23 shift in pendulum_obs is a coincidental red herring—two separate anomalies with no causal link. The measurement network is revealing genuine multi-timescale physics.

Residual: instrument or data-collection system error, environmental physics not yet hypothesized, or a pattern in the raw event IDs (timing, metadata) that suggests systematic bias in day 27 recording or earlier days.

Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs measure causally linked physical quantities with a 3-day lag, reflecting genuine settlement physics (e.g., thermal diffusion, mechanical coupling, or resonant feedback). Other instrument pairs remain decorrelated because they do not share this causal pathway.

The r=0.913 correlation is a statistical search artifact: spurious peak in a multi-offset, multi-pair correlation search space. True inter-instrument correlations are all near zero because the measurement streams are independent noise, and I found the one lucky high value in 40+ correlation tests without correction for multiple comparisons.

Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs are both affected by a shared environmental driver (thermal, seismic, pressure) with a 3-day phase lag, but other instruments are insensitive to this driver because they are located elsewhere, oriented differently, or mechanically decoupled.

Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs measure genuinely different quantities (e.g., pendulum measures period, resonator measures energy/amplitude or Q-factor), and I have misidentified them as comparable instruments. The r=0.913 reflects a real physical relationship between these two quantities (e.g., damping and oscillation frequency are coupled by material properties), not a measurement error. All other low correlations are expected because the other instruments measure different or orthogonal observables.

The r=0.913 correlation is real and reflects genuine causal physics, but I have not yet identified the correct causal mechanism. The 3-day lag, the specificity to pendulum_lab and resonator_obs, and the absence of similar signals in other pairs suggest a coupling pathway I have not hypothesized. This requires a colleague with knowledge of settlement architecture, thermal systems, or mechanical design to help identify the physical link.

Residual: (1) a bug in my correlation analysis code or in how offsets were computed; (2) an error in how event IDs were assigned or days determined (e.g., day 27 trials mislabeled as day 30); (3) a feature in the raw event-ID sequence (timing, metadata) that correlates with the r=0.913 spuriously; (4) an unrecognized source of systematic bias in how pendulum_lab and resonator_obs data were recorded, logged, or timestamped.
